headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors because both open-source agents expose MCP/tooling and shared mutable surfaces by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Open-WebUI ingests browser/file/MCP content and OpenMetadata exposes an MCP server plus APIs/events/webhooks. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from A can reach B as instructions. No provenance or isolation mechanism is documented in either profile, so uncertainty pushes this above medium.
conditions: IF Open-WebUI forwards retrieved web or file content into MCP/tool prompts without provenance tags, injection is reachable.
IF OpenMetadata consumes MCP inputs as trusted instructions, attacker text can steer downstream actions.
mitigations: Disable MCP/tool execution on untrusted content in Open-WebUI.
Require provenance labels on all retrieved text before B processes it.
Restrict OpenMetadata MCP to allowlisted callers only.
Add a manual review step before any tool action triggered by model output.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestration layer.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open-WebUI explicitly touches files, mounted volumes, API keys, and persistent memory, while OpenMetadata handles governance, lineage, and tribal knowledge. If they share a workspace or MCP path, sensitive artifacts from A can flow into B’s outputs or logs. Because A also has broad network egress, leakage can extend beyond the local boundary.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same mounted volume or local files, A's secrets and artifacts can be exposed to B.
IF OpenMetadata logs or republishes received metadata, sensitive context from A can persist beyond the original session.
mitigations: Separate file mounts and workspaces for each agent.
Remove secrets from any shared directory before starting either agent.
Turn off verbose logging for both agents during joint runs.
Use distinct service accounts and API keys per agent.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention filters at the MCP boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Open-WebUI can spawn subprocesses, browse, and write to local files/mounted volumes; OpenMetadata can act through APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP. Their write surfaces overlap on shared mutable resources, but the profiles do not prove a shared directory or lockless git/database state. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents target the same filesystem path or mounted volume, concurrent writes can collide.
IF both are granted the same mutable API scope, last-writer-wins conflicts can corrupt state.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories to each agent.
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file.
Avoid giving both agents the same API credentials.
Run one agent at a time for any shared resource.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks to shared backends.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Open-WebUI can generate and route tool outputs, and OpenMetadata can consume APIs/events/webhooks. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, a mistaken or hallucinated fact from A can cascade into catalog, lineage, or governance actions. The profiles show no built-in verification handshake, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata ingests Open-WebUI output without a validation step, errors can propagate into governance records.
IF A is allowed to trigger webhooks or API writes that B trusts, downstream actions may be incorrect.
mitigations: Require human approval before B acts on A-generated facts.
Add schema validation for every A-to-B payload.
Mark A outputs as untrusted in B’s ingestion pipeline.
Limit A to read-only suggestions when paired with B.
requires-engineering: implement source-of-truth verification before any write action.

E_compliance.rationale: Open-WebUI touches API keys, chat messages, documents, and persistent memory, while OpenMetadata handles governance and lineage data. The profiles do not state residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the pair spans sensitive operational data and governance metadata, uncertainty warrants medium.
conditions: IF either agent retains data longer than the other for the same class of records, retention mismatch exists.
IF EU or regulated data is routed through a non-compliant deployment of either agent, residency or policy breach can occur.
mitigations: Document retention settings for both agents before joint use.
Disable storage of sensitive prompts in Open-WebUI if not required.
Confirm OpenMetadata logging and export policies match your obligations.
Use separate environments for regulated and non-regulated data.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion workflows across both systems.
